articles.content:
GTA 6's fast-food hamburger chain, Burger Shot, is expanding with new locations across Florida starting this weekend thanks to a collaboration with Skinny Louie.

Last month, Burger Shot became available at the Kaseya Center, allowing fans to try the real version of the in-game restaurant during Miami Heat games, courtesy of a partnership with a fast-food joint known as Skinny Louie. The chain is now expanding this activation through its standalone stores across Florida. From November 13 to December 31, stores will feature Burger Shot signage, uniforms, and, of course, a menu themed after items in the game.

You can take a look at the menu and some images of the food below.

Skinny Louie's Burger Shot Menu

THE BLEEDER — TRIPLE
Three 100% Black Angus smash patties with yellow American cheese, crispy bacon, pickles, BBQ sauce, and ketchup.

BURGER SHOT — SINGLE

One 100% Black Angus smash patty with yellow American cheese, shredded lettuce, diced raw onions, and Burger Shot sauce.

BURGER SHOT — DOUBLE
Two 100% Black Angus smash patties with yellow American cheese, shredded lettuce, diced raw onions, and Burger Shot sauce.

CARAMEL MILKSHAKE

All of this just goes to show how big GTA 6 has gotten. There aren't many video game franchises that could completely command and rebrand a chain of restaurants, but GTA 6 certainly has that power. The game is already the most pre-ordered title in the history of Xbox and PlayStation's digital stores, and analysts estimate that the game has generated $1 billion in revenue ahead of launch.

GTA 6 will officially release next week on November 19 and players can start pre-loading right now. Rockstar has also been trickling out small clips of in-game footage, giving players a taste of what's to come when they load in to Vice City next week.

articles.title: The He Who Fights With Monsters Hardcover Books Are on Sale Before Black Friday
articles.content:
Amazon has kicked off its latest '3 for 2' sale on books ahead of Black Friday and there are some terrific new releases in there for LitRPG fans. If you haven't already scooped up the Dungeon Crawler Carl books, for example, now is a great time to do so for cheap. And if you're a fan of Travis Deverell's (AKA Shirtaloon) He Who Fights With Monsters series, you can also grab the first two hardcovers at a discount.

The first He Who Fights With Monsters hardcover was released earlier this year and the third book will be arriving next week. This series is my overall favorite LitRPG and a great read if you love Dungeon Crawler Carl.

He Who Fights With Monsters is fairly well-known in the LitRPG community already. There have been a total of 13 books released so far and they are all terrific. Similar to Dungeon Crawler Carl, there's a lot of humor and pop-culture references sprinkled throughout a relatively fast-paced story. It definitely leans more fantasy than sci-fi, so expect a lot more magic and a less actual science.

The story follows Jason Asano as he wakes up inside a hedge maze in a magical world with new powers and absolutely no hair on his body. His determined and off-balance attitude to his strange new predicament helps him to survive the likes of cannibals, monsters, and even personal relationships with ease. All-in-all, a fantastic book with a morally conflicted main character that you can’t help but love the whole way through. His dark and mysterious powers only make the story all the more interesting.

Also check out the Dungeon Crawler Carl books in the sale

Seeing as there are only two He Who Fights With Monsters books included in the sale, you will have to purchase one more eligible book to actually get the discount. I'd recommend checking out the Dungeon Crawler Carl hardcovers and the graphic novels, both of which are also buy 2, get 1 free. The first graphic novel is an easy recommendation if you already own these books, I gave it an 8 out of 10 in my review.

articles.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
articles.description: In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services. The post GitHub availability report: October 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
articles.content:
We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes)

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

What went wrong and why?

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How did we respond?

A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up.

Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident.

We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue.

We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover.

We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it.

We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded.

We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time.

We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on.

October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes)

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

What went wrong and why?

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How did we respond?

A surge of migration work overloaded a shared database, causing requests across github.com to fail or slow down.

Automated monitoring detected the failures and paged our on-call engineers.

The errors stopped on their own within minutes.

We declared an incident and paused enterprise migrations to prevent a recurrence while we investigated the cause.

Once a mitigation was deployed, we resumed migrations and resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We optimized the query GitHub Enterprise Importer sends to the database so that each one stays small and fixed in size.

We are automating importer backoff when the database is under strain, easing load before it can affect other GitHub services.

We are adding database alerts that flag queries doing much more work than usual and identify which query is responsible, so we can find and fix problems like this one faster.

October 07 15:14 and 17:17 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 11 minutes, and 47 minutes, respectively)

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

What went wrong and why?

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How did we respond?

Automated monitoring alerted us to failing writes, and we declared an incident.

Writes recovered when an established machine with correct records became leader and published correct settings.

We traced the cause to the new machine, resolved the first incident, and paused automated maintenance to prevent a repeat.

When a maintenance task did not honor the pause and the outage repeated, we declared a second incident.

Writes recovered when an established machine became leader again. We removed the new machine and resolved the second incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We improved how we retire database servers, so outdated records aren’t left behind.

We tightened controls on adding new machines that manage database routing, and making sure automated maintenance honors a pause.

We strengthened validation of database routing settings, so incorrect settings are caught before they take effect.

October 19 15:49 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 7 minutes)

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

What went wrong and why?

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How did we respond?

Automated alerts detected the failures, we declared an incident, and we traced the problem to the shared network link.

We routed the actions service away from some of its cache servers in that region, but the link was still over capacity.

We routed it away from the rest of those cache servers, and the link recovered.

We raised processing limits to clear the actions backlog, and we resolved the incident once all affected services had recovered.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We have limited how quickly this actions service can open new connections to its cache servers.

We are alerting on spikes in new connections from this service to identify and address the source sooner.

articles.title: Wolfenstein 3 Confirmed to Be in Development at MachineGames
articles.description: As part of the Xbox's 25th anniversary celebration at Xbox Fanfest in Seattle today, developer MachineGames confirmed what had long been rumored: that Wolfenstein 3 is in development.
articles.content:
As part of the Xbox's 25th anniversary celebration at Xbox Fanfest in Seattle today, developer MachineGames confirmed what had long been rumored: that Wolfenstein 3 is in development.

MachineGames will once again be developing it. Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus was released to rave reviews in 2017, but MachineGames then put the series on hold to develop 2024's absolutely stellar Indiana Jones and the Great Circle.

But now, Wolfenstein is back on the front burner at the Swedish studio. "Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at Machine Games," Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed on X. "One of gaming’s most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more."

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more. https://t.co/YyX8LrbTvh

— ASHA (@asha_shar) November 12, 2026

MachineGames added on to Sharma's post, which shows a page of the Wolfenstein 3 script, saying simply, "His reputation precedes him," referring to the action described on the script page. "Wolfenstein 3 is in production." The developers also confirmed that actors Brian Bloom (as B.J. Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (as Grace Walker) will return via a photo of the pair in the developer's motion-capture studio.

Wolfenstein 3 shouldn't come as much of a surprise. Last year, in an interview with Noclip, MachineGames studio head Jerk Gustafsson said the team had "always seen [BJ's story] as a trilogy," adding: "That journey for BJ, even during those first weeks at [id Software], when we mapped out New Order — we still had the plan for at least [BJ], what would happen in the second one and what would happen in the third one.

"I think that's important to say, because⁠ — at least, I hope ⁠— we're not done with Wolfenstein yet. We have a story to tell."

That's not all that Wolfenstein fans have to look forward to, as the pioneering first-person shooter series is also being developed into a TV series at Amazon. Xbox's official 25th anniversary is this Sunday, November 15.

articles.title: DOJ takes aim at $1.2B in Binance loot as FBI disrupts North Korean scam
articles.description: ‘FaceStealer’ scam tied to $400M+ theft, 900+ webcam recordings
articles.content:
The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft.

The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months.

It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks.

900+ faces stolen

The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers.

Here’s how the attack works.

First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible.

“You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles.

“They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday.

The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite.

Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told.

“When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.”

‘You’re on mute’ as a social engineering vector

The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix.

Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam.

The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet, which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.

“The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.”

Binance heist update

The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.

Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”

Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

articles.title: Microsoft struggling to fix massive cloud outage that's taken down email and Intune
articles.description: ‘Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief’
articles.content:
Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed.

The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too.

On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”

The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.”

According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.”

“We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote.

But those efforts may not be working.

“We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.”

The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted.

Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.”

But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration.

This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ®

UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they " initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic."

So not usefully healthy at all, then.

"We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised.

articles.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
articles.description: Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them. The post Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
articles.content:
How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

Define one job and when it applies

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

---
name: proof-agent
description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues.
---

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

Keep project configuration out of the skill

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

project:
name: "support-desk"
store_name: "support_metric_store"

platform:
engine: "duckdb"
pipeline_framework: "spark_python"
duckdb_dir: "warehouse"

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

Share execution paths between skills

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

Put checks and approval points in the workflow

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Package for each agent client, then verify its setup

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files:.claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code,.cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and.github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

node scripts/package.mjs --check

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Three practices for building agent skills

Put business context in one file. Keep project-specific names, schemas, and conventions in a manifest, and have each skill read it instead of duplicating those facts. This gives the team one visible place to update configuration.

Give related skills one consistent way to use the platform. Have related skills use the same path to run queries, jobs, and schema changes instead of each defining its own commands and connection logic. This makes the workflow’s access easier to understand and its behavior easier to check in each client.

Use instructions to guide the work, and checks to verify it. A skill can tell an agent which standards to follow and when to ask for approval. Add human review at decisions that need context or judgment, and use tests and CI checks to catch issues before a change moves forward. If a check must block a merge or deployment, configure that requirement in your repository’s rules.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

articles.title: Skydance Owning Both Warner Bros. and Paramount Could Open the Door to a Future of Crossover Slop
articles.description: Skydance owning the IP of both Warner Bros. and Paramount opens the door to them possibly doing crossover films one day, a future where $300 million glorified fan fic films could be the next big thing.
articles.content:
What the future holds for DC Studios in a post-James Gunn and Peter Safran world is anyone’s guess at the moment. Perhaps we’ll know more once incoming DC Studios President and Chief Creative Officer Jeremy Latcham assumes command December 1, but I assume there may not be any new film or TV slates officially announced until after the New Year.

The biggest question, obviously, is whether the new Skydance-operated regime will reboot Gunn’s DCU, with some reports claiming that might be the case. Skydance is $87 billion in debt and looking to cut costs and maximize profits across the board. Post-merger, Skydance now has all of the Paramount intellectual property at their disposal to exploit as well as the entire Warner Bros. library.

So how might such a debt-riddled corporation start producing films that seem like safer commercial bets than, say, a Clayface movie (which was a modest success for DC Studios)? They will obviously lean on their most recognizable, bestselling brands ( hi, Batman! ), but Skydance now owning the IP of both studios opens the door to them possibly doing crossover films one day.

That was what many fans thought might happen with Disney and Fox properties after those studios merged, but audiences are only getting their first real taste of that crossover potential with Avengers: Doomsday. That acquisition was completed seven years ago, and I can’t see Skydance wanting to wait that long to jumpstart audience interest in all the new toys they have to play with.

Mind you, I’m not advocating for crossover films between Warner Bros. and Paramount IP, but it does seem like something someone at Skydance has to at least consider. A live-action Batman meets the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie might sound ridiculous, but those two properties have already done animated film and comic book crossovers, so maybe it’s not as crazy as it sounds.

Of course, Paramount has yet to even make a proper Transformers/G.I. Joe crossover movie and they’ve had those properties in-house for ages. There would certainly be a lot of legal entanglements still involved in any Warners/Paramount crossover project despite Skydance owning both studios – producers’ existing deals, credits, etc. – but when you owe $87 billion, maybe kicking around huge event movie ideas like a franchise crossover might not be too crazy to consider.

Granted, such crossovers would open the door to Hollywood essentially making fan fic films, but they’re high-concept and marketable to mass audiences. A studio exec could simply type a prompt into AI and have it spit out a list of potential crossover movies, which I feel certain someone at Skydance must have already done.

Are we looking at a future where, say, the Justice League teams with the Autobots to stop Lex Luthor and the Decepticons? Where the Terminator is sent into the Matrix or the Green Lantern Corps teams with Starfleet to thwart some multiversal threat? Could the IMF team from Mission: Impossible recruit members of the Suicide Squad? Freddy Krueger vs. Ghostface? The Conjuring investigators visit a household from Paranormal Activity? Aquaman meets SpongeBob? Krypto pals around with Paw Patrol? What if that mysterious evil from Smile found its way to Gotham City and drew the attention of a certain Clown Prince of Crime?

I think you get the idea of where this could go. Crossovers, of course, are nothing new. The Universal Monsters were doing that decades ago. Who Framed Roger Rabbit? famously teamed Looney Tunes and Disney characters. More recently, The LEGO Movie franchise saw Superman, Lando Calrissian and Gandalf all share the screen, while the Ready Player One movie enlisted nearly every major pop culture IP under the sun.

The likelihood of Warners-Paramount crossover films happening seems more possible now that so much IP is owned by the same giant media company. Perhaps such intermingling between these IPs will never happen (or not to the scale I’ve suggested here) … or maybe I just foretold a future where crossover slop and $300 million glorified fan fic films are the next big thing. Maybe we’re looking at a cinematic phase of gods and monsters after all, just not the ones we expected.

articles.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Had Third Affair With Another Employee
articles.description: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned today amid a scandal involving an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and an executive that reported to him. Now, it's been reported that Huang allegedly had an affair with a second employee.
articles.content:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned today amid a scandal involving an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and an executive that reported to him. Now, it's been reported that Huang allegedly had an affair with a second employee.

Huang allegedly had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two sources inside Nvidia and reported by Reuters. However, Reuters hasn't named the second employee, and attempts to reach her were not successful.

This third revelation comes just hours after Huang resigned from Nvidia, following an internal investigation that kicked off on Sunday. Huang himself came out and admitted to one of the affairs in a letter sent to Nvidia staff and obtained by The BBC. Then, following a meeting where Nvidia's board weighed ousting Huang, the former CEO resigned.

In the meantime, Nvidia's board has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while the company searches for a new leader. Nvidia is considering both internal and external applicants, but there has been talk that Apple Senior Vice President of Hardware Technlogy Johny Srouji is being considered for the role, according to MacRumors.

As for Huang itself, it's not clear where he's going to end up, or what he's going to do going forward. Last night, Elon Musk posted on X that it "would be an honor" to hire Huang... but it's doubtful that he'd end up at any of Musk's companies.

Either way, Huang has been leading Nvidia since 1993, and has seen the company grow from being a niche gaming hardware company to the backbone of the entire AI industry. His resignation is going to send shockwaves throughout the entire tech biz. One of the biggest casualties might end up being PC gaming altogether. After all, Nvidia makes up for a massive 73% of Steam's install base, according to the latest Steam Hardware survey, but the company still dropped gaming from its earnings reports earlier this year. And, now with Jensen's departure, it's unlikely that PC hardware is going to get the same level of support.

articles.title: Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view
articles.description: 'Intelligent eyewear' has a built-in camera and mic, but there's a recording light to warn you and some stern legalese to discourage abuse
articles.content:
It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy.

As announced Thursday, Google has decided not to make wearables itself, instead turning Samsung and eyeglass makers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Like most of the rest of this generation of smart glasses, none of the nine styles available feature heads-up displays, just cameras and audio feedback from Gemini.

Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video.

Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times.

Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10.

Google promises privacy

The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them.

Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “ pervert glasses.”

Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns.

As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features.

“We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us.

The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. Google told us it does save audio recordings and transcripts of conversations with Gemini that users create while wearing the glasses but again insists that those aren’t used to train its AI models.

We asked about serving ads too, but Google’s responses didn't address the topic.

Lucky for those in range of a pair of Google glasses when wearers ask Gemini to interpret images captured by the device's camera, the tech specs redact the faces of strangers before they’re transmitted. Google told us that face redaction doesn’t apply to photos or videos saved to a wearer’s camera roll.

Google’s terms of use require users not to record others without permission, or in "sensitive places." If users ignore that requirement, the company reserves the right to brick their devices. Another restriction means Google won't allow apps that use the glasses for real-time streaming or facial recognition into its Play app store.

Given that it remains possible to use the glasses to store recordings of people around a wearer, it’s safe to assume non real-time facial recognition is still a possibility. Creeps will doubtless use such loopholes to behave abominably. ®

articles.title: A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs
articles.description: Anthropic sets behavior standards to protect Claude from rough treatment
articles.content:
If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable, a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude.

Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults.

Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate.

How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers).

A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request.

"Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style."

The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models."

The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research.

While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition.

Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage.

Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model.

Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper, "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses.

Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project, as did numerous social media users.

Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse.

Chris Donnelly, Searchable CEO and co-founder, endorsed Anthropic's change of terms, suggesting that it could help make human interaction more civil.

"For me, Anthropic's policy change is a positive move," Donnelly said in a statement. "It should help people get more out of chatbots, and it helps curb the kind of derogatory behavior that previous research suggests can spill over into how people talk to each other." ®

articles.title: Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster
articles.description: Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather The post Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather than keeping its most capable model running across an entire session, Google is pairing Hydrogen with the more powerful Gemini 4 Carbon and switching between the two as the work progresses.

The company says the combination gets nearly the same results as running Carbon on its own while using 24% less quota and finishing tasks 19% faster.

How Orchestrator handles the work

The switching runs through Orchestrator, a new feature in Google’s Antigravity development environment, where Carbon takes on the more demanding reasoning, including architecture and debugging, while Hydrogen handles code changes and testing.

Carbon might work through a repository to figure out how to implement a feature and then hand the actual coding to Hydrogen, stepping back in when a failing test calls for rethinking the approach before passing execution back.

Clement Farabet, VP, AI engineering at Google DeepMind, calls the combination “a huge unlock for agentic coding” in a post on X.

Varun Mohan, who leads Google’s Antigravity team, says in a separate post that pairing Hydrogen with Orchestrator and swarms has become “very popular internally.”

Where Google’s numbers don’t match

Google’s own benchmark reporting doesn’t quite line up, since the main Gemini announcement cites Terminal-Bench 4.0 while the Antigravity announcement references version 4.1.

The company also hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate, a per-task breakdown or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.

…hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate… or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.

Hydrogen outscores a pricier model

Google describes Hydrogen as a “daily driver for agentic workflows,” and it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with those rates holding across its full million-token context window.

The model is available through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, as well as the Gemini app and Google Search.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Hydrogen scores 51 at its default high thinking level, just ahead of the more expensive Gemini 4 Argon at 50. Turning the reasoning effort up to Google’s new xhigh setting brings Hydrogen’s score to 54, although the additional reasoning can increase token consumption and processing time.

Argon was Google’s flagship when it launched on September 30, but Gemini 4 Carbon surpassed it on most published benchmarks following its October 28 release. Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up with what passed for frontier performance just weeks ago.

Google also claims Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default setting, with its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score reaching 57% against Flash’s 18.2%. The company reports more than a fivefold reduction in fabricated claims.

Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up…

The cost of switching models

Google hasn’t disclosed how Orchestrator decides when to switch models or what those handoffs cost in additional tokens and latency.

For now, Orchestrator is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, with support for more models and subscription tiers planned. Hydrogen is rolling out to paid Antigravity users, with broader availability expected.

articles.title: Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk.
articles.description: Coding agents are pretty good at working in parallel: one writes a new API endpoint, another updates the tests, while The post Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Coding agents are pretty good at working in parallel: one writes a new API endpoint, another updates the tests, while a third fixes a bug elsewhere in the codebase. However, they’re not quite so adept at knowing what their coding counterparts are doing — put several on one project and they duplicate work, trip over each other’s changes, and leave the developer firefighting the fiasco that follows.

That’s why the major AI labs and coding-tool makers have all been looking for ways to bring order to their agent fleets, albeit with slightly different approaches.

This week alone, Google and Cursor both debuted features designed to keep agents from tripping over each other, but at different scales. Google’s Swarm organizes the agents working for a single developer, while Cursor’s multiplayer Projects lets agents working for different colleagues coordinate with each other.

Cursor gets teammates’ agents talking

Cursor first debuted Projects back in September, giving developers a way to hand a larger job to a coordinator agent that breaks it into tasks and delegates them to worker agents.

Then on Tuesday, the company, which Elon Musk’s SpaceX acquired for $60 billion in August, unveiled multiplayer functionality for Projects. Developers can now invite teammates into a project, where each person gets their own coordinator and workers.

Cursor coordinators exchange messages across teammates’ tasks.

Everyone’s agents work from the same task board and project documents, and their coordinators can message each other directly to share plans, flag overlaps and more.

Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves.

Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves. If one teammate’s agents are changing a database schema and another’s are building a feature that depends on it, their coordinators can agree on which change needs to land first.

Antigravity, for its part, is Google’s counterpart to Cursor. It’s where Google has consolidated various other coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity and begun winding down Jules, its background coding agent.

On the same day Cursor unveiled multiplayer Projects, Google rolled out Gemini 4 Carbon in Antigravity, alongside a preview of its own approach to coordinating coding agents. Dubbed Swarm (stylized as /swarm), it lets a developer hand one assignment to a coordinator that then splits it among worker agents and assigns a verifier to check their changes. The workers can message each other on a shared board, so they can coordinate their changes as they go.

For example, a company that wants to change how its online checkout system verifies authentication tokens could use Swarm to split the work. One agent updates the authentication middleware while another updates the token verifier. They can work in separate Git worktrees, use the board to agree on how their changes fit together, and hand them off to a verifier for testing.

Swarm agents split and verify a token migration.

Taking to X on Tuesday, Varun Mohan, director of software engineering at Google DeepMind, said Swarm gives developers a convenient way to put multiple agents on a complex task, adding that Google staff were already using Swarm to take on larger jobs internally.

“The alpha from using swarms is ridiculous,” Mohan writes. “We have folks using swarms of 100s of agents to build large systems and products from scratch with a single prompt.”

Logan Kilpatrick, a member of technical staff at Google DeepMind, said on X that seeing swarm outputs had been ‘really impressive,’ and that they offered ‘a new scaling dimension for AI!”

“A new scaling dimension for AI!”

This, ultimately, gets to the crux of how each of these companies has tackled agent coordination.

When agents work for different people

Antigravity’s Swarm takes one developer’s assignment and gives the agents handling it a way to talk as they work. Cursor’s multiplayer Projects, meanwhile, takes assignments from different teammates and lets their coordinators talk across those assignments

That’s the distinction Cursor product manager Aryaman Khandelwal is keen to draw in Tuesday’s announcement.

“Multi-agent systems have so far served one person. Projects is a multi-agent system built for a whole team.”

“Multi-agent systems have so far served one person,” Khandelwal writes. “Projects is a multi-agent system built for a whole team.”

A quick peek across the AI coding landscape shows how others have approached agent coordination — including Anthropic. Its still-experimental Claude Code Agent Teams gives agents working on a common assignment a shared task list and a way to message each other. And recently, the company added cross-session messaging to Claude Code, so sessions started separately can exchange findings or warn each other about changes. But those sessions still belong to the same developer.

In October, GitHub put Projects in the Copilot app into public preview, giving developers a way to hand Copilot a goal that spans repositories and have it distribute the work across agents. AWS’s Kiro Crew bots, meanwhile, which launched last week, can start several sessions, steer them as they run and pull their results together.

Separately, Anthropic and OpenAI have also built agents that teammates can use together. Anthropic introduced Claude Tag in June, letting people in a Slack channel delegate to a shared Claude. OpenAI’s ChatGPT workspace agents, announced in April, can be used and maintained by multiple colleagues.

Community concerns: Spreading mistakes

However, some in the community raised concerns that letting teammates’ agents talk could spread one agent’s mistakes across the whole team, especially if each person’s agents follow different rules, and that an agent could request information it shouldn’t have access to. Khandelwal, though, responded that multiplayer Projects lets teams define shared rules and skills for everyone in a project. On the access part, Cursor’s documentation says agents treat messages from teammates’ agents as untrusted input and ask before sharing a person’s private files or connector data. A teammate’s message is handled in a separate chat, which Cursor says never shares secrets or credentials. The Projects documentation doesn’t say whether admins can set different rules for those exchanges based on a teammate’s role.

Separately, fresh research suggests that teams of per-user agents can struggle. In a study published Wednesday, researchers in Anthropic’s Fellows Program tested what happens when multiple users each delegate to their own agent and those agents share a resource, in four simulated environments that included a code merge queue. In every environment, group outcomes were worse than when a single agent served everyone, by roughly 10 to 45 percentage points for Anthropic’s Claude models, even when each user’s agents could message each other. Agents stalled as teams grew, overrode other users’ requests, and made unsupported claims about what other people wanted. Some fixes helped, such as appointing a lead agent or blocking an agent from acting until it had read its messages, but which ones worked depended on the task.

All in all, these various launches this year show a push to make it easier for teams to delegate work and keep track of what their agents are doing. With multiplayer mode in Projects, Cursor is tackling a specific part of that problem.

Parker Smith, who works in engineering for Cursor’s parent company SpaceXSI, says the point is really just to keep agents moving without unnecessary delays.

“Agents move fast, having a blocker on peer context is too slow,” Smith writes on X. “Multiplayer projects allow your agent to grab all the context it needs from your coworkers agents without needing to involve you.”

Cursor’s multiplayer Projects is in beta now for users on a team account, while Google’s Swarm is in preview for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

articles.content:
Yandex, sometimes called Russia’s Google, has updated its customers in the wake of extensive damage to its data centers in drone strikes. In a blog post this week, the firm’s cloud business boasted that it had “restored access to more than 97% of customer data” [machine translation]. That might sound like a great success, but in the small print, as highlighted by The Register, there’s the admission “the remaining 2.84% cannot be restored due to critical damage to equipment.”

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

The custom AI ASIC state of play

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Data centers operated by Yandex have been under attack from Ukrainian drones for several weeks now. We covered reports about withering online troll activity and online payment system disruption last month. We know of at least three Yandex locations that have been damaged by Ukrainian drone assaults to date.

The recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of users who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups. When talking about the 2.84% of data that cannot be restored, it says that was partly due to “the lack of customer backups on the platform.” In contrast, those who made use of the Yandex Cloud backup tools “did not lose any data,” says the firm.

Yandex has now changed the backup policy, so that “currently, all virtual machines created in Yandex Cloud work with the backup function enabled by default.” Even if Putin decides to end his war on Ukraine, it might be beneficial to stick with a backup-by-default policy. Users are advised to have their own data backup systems in addition to the cloud. Following the 3-2-1 backup strategy, for example.

Yandex is also opening a new ru-central1-f availability zone at a new location. This is designed to improve the cloud’s fault tolerance and disaster resilience. articles.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
articles.description: Meanwhile, a group of nonprofits sue AI giants and cite AI-driven cyberattacks
articles.content:
OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these.

“We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address.

The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.”

However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations. “Also very important is product.”

This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform.

Red Team, which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths.

It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws.

The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory, automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber. The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production.

“This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said.

Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models.

The lawsuit, filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face, gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics, and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents.

“Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

articles.title: Valheim Is Getting a Comic Book Series, and It Looks Badass
articles.description: Valheim is expanding beyond video games once again, this time with an official comic book series featuring an impressive lineup of talent from Marvel, DC, television, and animation.
articles.content:
Valheim is expanding beyond video games once again, this time with an official comic book series featuring an impressive lineup of talent from Marvel, DC, television, and animation.

Developer Iron Gate Studio has teamed up with GUNGNIR Books and MOOD Publishing to bring its Viking survival game to comics, with the first release planned for the first quarter of 2027. The multi-issue series will feature original stories set in the world of Valheim, rather than simply retelling the events of the game.

The writing team certainly has a pretty impressive portfolio that bodes well for the series. It includes Steve Orlando (Wonder Woman, Avengers), Deric A. Hughes and Ben Raab (Quantum Leap), J. Holtham (The Handmaid's Tale, Supergirl), Brea Grant (12 Hour Shift), Tim Sheridan (Masters of the Universe), and Olan Rogers (Final Space). They're joined by TD Orel, Chris Klian, Andrew Sanders, and GUNGNIR Books founder Matthew Medney.

On the art side, Scott Oakley, Vanessa Del Rey, Lucas Pereira, and Mario Del Pennino are among the confirmed artists, with Mohamad Samah overseeing production design. More talent is expected to be announced.

According to the announcement, the series will explore the mythology of Valheim's mysterious tenth Norse realm, introducing new adventures and perspectives on its gods, monsters, and dangerous environments. Expect plenty of exploration, survival, and presumably some very unfortunate encounters with the local wildlife.

This is Valheim, and we're going to make it epic. “Valheim is one of those rare worlds that feels like it existed long before we ever discovered it. There are gods, monsters, entire civilizations, and a mythology so rich that the stories we can tell feel almost endless," said Matthew Medney from GUNGNIR Books. "For us, the opportunity to work alongside Iron Gate and MOOD Publishing to bring this universe into comics is extraordinary. And we've assembled an absolute army of creative talent to do it. We're not interested in simply retelling what millions of players have already experienced. We want to explore the legends that haven't been told, the corners of this world that haven't been seen, and create something that feels worthy of the incredible universe Iron Gate built. This is Valheim, and we're going to make it epic."

The comic marks another expansion for Valheim, which has now sold more than 17 million copies worldwide since launching into Steam Early Access in February 2021. The game has already made the jump to tabletop gaming with Valheim: The Board Game, also developed in partnership with MOOD Publishing.

For now, there's no specific release date beyond Q1 2027, and details about individual issues, collectible editions, and how fans can get involved are still to come. In the meantime, Valheim players can look forward to exploring the tenth realm without having to worry about keeping their food buffs topped up. Which, frankly, sounds rather nice.

articles.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
articles.description: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “pote
articles.content:
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” 

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” 

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. 

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. 

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. 

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

Four minutes of new Fable gameplay has been released by Xbox, showing off more of the game's combat.

The footage was released personally by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma as part of a larger celebration for the company's 25th anniversary. The gameplay shows off a bunch of combat, highlighting not only standard swordplay, but also ranged attacks and unique moves that can be performed using magic. The gameplay was captured on PC using ultra graphics settings and concludes with the protagonist stumbling upon an incredibly sinister-looking tomb or coffin.

Fable was, of course, meant to have been released this fall. However, Xbox made the smart decision to delay the game to February. Although the team says the delay wasn't done specifically in an effort to avoid GTA 6, it was likely a nice benefit. Microsoft still had plenty of releases this autumn thanks to Modern Warfare 4 and Gears of War: E-Day, so it was wise to give Fable some more room to breathe. The game was announced all the way back in 2020, but has been in some form of development at Playground Games for nearly a decade.

Forza Horizon studio Playground Games is leading the charge on the title, though it has recruited a bunch of talent from around the industry so that it is well-equipped to build an RPG. Fable is one of the most anticipated games on Xbox's slate, partially because it's one of the most beloved RPG franchises out there, and Microsoft is looking for a big win in the AAA space outside of shooters.

Fable is also coming to PS5, as it had been previously announced for the platform. It'll be interesting to see what happens if the game performs well on the platform. Xbox is trying to lean more into exclusivity, but it unfortunately didn't seem to pay off for Gears of War: E-Day. Here's hoping Fable is worth the wait and pays off on Microsoft's investments.
