articles.content:
4 Min Read

I Am Artemis Katie Spicer

For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history.

NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028.

NASA/Bill Strafford

Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives.

“I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.”

Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory, performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists.

“I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said.

From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station. She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed. It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations.

Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018. The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her. Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications.

“Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said. “On my own, I studied engineering principles. I passed boards and certification tests. I learned to speak ‘engineer!’”

Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight.

Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface.

“I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

articles.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
articles.description: Lego fans demand answers as outage approaches a week with no confirmed cause
articles.content:
Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures.

The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone.

Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11.

"We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

"Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

"This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible."

The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond.

Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6.

"Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit.

"They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page."

BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures.

The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020.

At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures.

The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service.

For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ®

articles.title: Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis
articles.description: The competition is circling like vultures
articles.content:
Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler.

For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it.

Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much.

Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit.

CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead.

And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas.

A marred reputation

One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea.

It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer.

Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom.

After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful.

One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country.

The consequences of controversy

When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself.

Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat.

Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries.

Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. Regardless, with Nvidia’s reputation marred and its future shrouded in uncertainty, once loyal customers may be more willing to explore alternative providers.

There are certainly plenty to choose from. Amid a surge in custom AI chips from the likes of Broadcom, Marvel, and others, Nvidia’s main advantage wasn’t so much technological as it was simply considered a safe bet.

AMD is the most obvious winner here. As we reported earlier this year, the House of Zen’s GPU tech has already surpassed Nvidia’s, at least on paper. What’s more, the company has a long and unblemished relationship serving the US government. AMD’s chips now power two of the Department of Energy’s three largest and most sensitive supercomputers.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers with sufficient cashflow – think Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta – may seek to insulate themselves from Huang’s fallout by investing more heavily in homegrown silicon and offering it to customers.

Then there's the threat from the man himself. Huang's ambitions and influence are such that he's unlikely to fade into obscurity. He may disappear from the spotlight while things blow over, but it’s a pretty sure bet that he’ll pop up at a new company eventually, and will still have enough sway to poach some of Nvidia’s top engineers. ®

articles.title: ‘Maybe We’ve Gone a Step Too Far’ — Ocarina of Time Remake Producer Reveals the Game's ReDeads Were Originally Supposed to Be Even Scarier
articles.description: Producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained why the development team behind the Ocarina of Time Remake toned down the ReDeads to make them less scary.
articles.content:
Producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained why the development team behind the Ocarina of Time Remake toned down the ReDeads to make them less scary.

If you grew up playing the original Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64, you were probably traumatized by some of the game’s famously frightening enemies like the Gibdos, ReDeads, and Dead Hands. These last two were particularly terrifying for young players at the time — partially because we were still kids, and partially due to the N64’s graphical limitations that forced our minds to fill in the visual gaps in the monsters’ designs.

These enemies were a particular talking point when the Remake was first announced. Some players were doubtful that this new game could truly capture the terror of the original monsters, since a) it’s a game that’s also supposed to appeal to children and b) the updated graphics of modern Nintendo consoles don’t necessarily allow for the ‘fear of the unknown’ phenomena afforded to low-fidelity titles like 1999's Silent Hill. (There’s an entire genre of indie horror games that pursue this aesthetic for a reason, after all.)

Speaking with Gamespot, producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained that the Remake’s updated graphics actually made the ReDeads extremely scary at first. And while the development team was supposedly enthusiastic about this aspect of the project, he and fellow producer Eiji Aonuma felt that this detail wasn’t necessarily true to the original experience of the first game.

"With this remake, the graphics are a lot improved, and so the ReDead – the sound, the graphics, and the movement – ended up being very, very scary,” Fujibayashi said. “And the staff wanted to make this in service of making a good gameplay experience. But from our perspective, taking a step back, we felt like, ‘Let's remember the experience that we don't want to change, and taking that into consideration, maybe we've gone a step too far, so let's dial it back.’"

That being said, plenty of players feel that the Remake’s ReDeads are still sufficiently terrifying. Social media is rife with hilarious reactions from fans’ first encounters with the enemies, with both Western and Japanese players having a “nope, f**k this,” mentality after first coming across them in the game.

articles.title: Doom Developer id Software Confirms Work on New Game, Will Be Directed by Hugo Martin
articles.description: At Xbox's 25th anniversary celebration at its Fan Fest event in Seattle, id Software confirmed that it is working on a new game, wrapping up last year's Doom: The Dark Ages with the release of the upcoming Slaughter Mode on November 16.
articles.content:
At Xbox's 25th anniversary celebration at its Fan Fest event in Seattle, id Software confirmed that it is working on a new game, wrapping up last year's Doom: The Dark Ages with the release of the upcoming Slaughter Mode on November 16.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma made the announcement on her X account, posting, "Few studios have shaped the first-person shooter genre as much as id Software. Slaughter Mode comes to DOOM: The Dark Ages | Revelations on November 16, and the team is already working on its next game." id itself also posted, saying, "We're incredibly excited about our next project, a new game from our teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin. It'll be some time before we're ready to share more but we can't wait for you to see what we're working on."

Whether that next project is more Doom, or perhaps id returning to its other big franchise, Quake, remains to be seen. Or it might be neither of those and could be something new entirely. Although it's worth noting that id Software is under Xbox's Bethesda arm, and Bethesda boss Jill Braff recently told its development teams that "we are shifting from a planning model primarily centered on what's next for each independent studio to one that focuses on our strongest franchises and determining the content roadmap that best serves our players and Bethesda as a whole." So perhaps Quake or a fourth Doom game are the more likely options?

That remains to be seen, but what the last decade has proven is that Martin and the id Software team are very good at what they do. Doom (2016) successfully rebooted a dormant franchise, while Doom Eternal stood on its shoulders, and then Doom: The Dark Ages brought the focus back to the ground. All three were excellent.

Doom: The Dark Ages' Slaughter Mode, meanwhile, is an endless single-player mode that will be added as a free update for those who've purchased Doom: The Dark Ages - Revelations DLC, which we reviewed and loved.

articles.title: As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns, the Future of GeForce Hangs in the Balance
articles.description: After 33 years, Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia, following a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy. And while this has all kinds of implications for the economy as a whole, in our own little world of PC gaming, it's looking increasingly unlikely that GeForce is going to get much attention
articles.content:
After 33 years, Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia, following a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy. This has all kinds of implications for the economy as a whole but Huang's exit will certainly have a ripple effect on the world of PC gaming, too. With Nvidia CFO Collette Kress stepping in as interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent replacement, it's looking increasingly unlikely that GeForce is going to get much attention going forward.

Kress joined Nvidia in 2013, as the GeForce GTX 780 was coming out, and has helped guide the company through its transformation into a data center and AI powerhouse. Before Nvidia, she was at Cisco as the CFO of Business Technology and Operations Finance, and before that, she was CFO of the Servers and Tools Group at Microsoft. Her history, combined with Nvidia's current trajectory, means that AI is still going to be Nvidia's main business. After all, Nvidia has made hundreds of billions of dollars pursuing AI, so having a CFO in charge, even in the interim, probably means Team Green is going to push even harder for the AI market.

On the surface, then, nothing would really be changing for the company. I've been covering Nvidia for more than a decade now, and I've watched in real time as GeForce has become a smaller and smaller part of its CES showcases. Just this year, Nvidia straight up dropped gaming from its earnings reports, combining the category with "edge computing," along with robotics and mobile computing.

Nvidia almost certainly would have continued deprioritizing GeForce, regardless of Huang's exit. The difference, though, is that Huang has been with Nvidia from the beginning, when it was primarily a gaming company. Despite pushing AI as the centerpiece of Nvidia's mission since at least 2016, he at least recognized that gaming was great for Nvidia's public image and would throw gamers a bone every now and then.

To be clear, I don't think Nvidia is going to be exiting the gaming business any time soon. Nvidia has a stranglehold on the entire PC gaming market, and it'd be bad business to walk away from a space where they have a near monopoly. There will still probably be new GeForce cards coming out — it's likely the RTX 60 series will come out in 2028 — but I think there's a real risk of Nvidia growing complacent with its market share and releasing worse products as the company invests most of its R&D into its data center business.

There had already been signs of things getting worse for PC gamers. The RTX 50 series had a couple of duds and had brutal price hikes across the board. But no matter how you look at it, Nvidia's current-generation graphics cards are still the best in the business and are supported by a wide swath of software that is unmatched by AMD and Intel.

I would love to be proven wrong, but I could see GeForce falling into a slump parallel to Intel's after Skylake in 2015, when Team Blue followed its consumer CPUs with more and more rebadges of the same architecture (Kaby Lake, Coffee Lake, etc.) because it had consumer market dominance and simply made more money elsewhere. During that time, Intel also had a transitional CEO, Brian Krzanich, who helped Intel expand into other industries.

AMD could get its act together and come out with something awesome to compete, just like it did with Ryzen in 2017. But AMD CEO Lisa Su has said in a recent interview with Yahoo Finance that "we are a data-center first company," so the odds of that happening are looking grim.

The real casualties from the fallout are probably going to be the weirder gaming releases that Nvidia sprinkles throughout the year. In January, that was G-Sync Pulsar, a new form of G-Sync, which flickers the backlight of your gaming monitor to trick your eyes into thinking the display is running at a higher refresh rate. That technology was essentially a passion project that had been cooking in the background for years before finally landing in a few gaming monitors at CES 2026. Tto this day I wish it was found in more gaming monitors.

I suspect GeForce is going to look a lot different than it does now in a few years. If Nvidia ends up with a CEO who has a career history anything like Kress's, I'd expect less of a focus on GPUs you can slot into your gaming PC, and more of a focus on funneling more GPUs into data centers. I just hope that I'm wrong.

articles.title: AI Usage Up, PS6 and Xbox Helix Development Still Low in Newest GDC Dev Survey
articles.description: GDC Festival of Gaming organizers released the data from their 15th annual game developer survey, the State of the Game Industry report. Over 2600 game developers anonymously responded, and the results show increased generative AI usage, not too many developers working on PlayStation 6 or Xbox Proje
articles.content:
GDC Festival of Gaming organizers released the data from their 15th annual game developer survey, the State of the Game Industry report. Over 2,600 game developers anonymously responded, and the results show increased generative AI usage, not too many developers working on PlayStation 6 or Xbox Project Helix next-gen projects as of yet, an increase in the number of developers in a union, and more.

"40% of game industry professionals report using generative AI tools as part of their job, up four points from the previous survey," GDC reported. "57% of AI adopters use it daily. Usage is highest among those working at mobile-only studios (70%) and those working on free-to-play games (58%). Company policy tends to vary significantly by company size, with 27% of AAA workers feeling encouraged or pressured to use generative AI, compared to only 9% of indie studio workers."

However, the report continued, "despite the industry’s increased adoption of generative AI, its use remains polarizing; 55% of respondents felt that it has a negative impact on games, which is consistent with 54% from the previous survey. Responses suggest that game industry professionals are forming nuanced stances on the topic. For instance, some respondents wrote that they see value in using generative AI tools for repetitive tasks, research, and prototyping, but others cited environmental, psychological, and societal concerns for their hesitation to use such tools. Others pondered whether generative AI could be an equalizer for marginalized and excluded groups struggling with cost, geography, or access."

Meanwhile, 10% of survey respondents are currently developing for PS6, with 8% currently working on Xbox's Project Helix. VR, augumented reality, or mixed reality game development is down to 3% of people surveyed, while Switch 2 development interest is up almost 10% to 47% this year.

Interestingly, overall support in the US for game industry worker unionization was down a tad, from 82% to 80%, but more respondents reported being part of a union – 15% this year compared to 12% last year.

Finally and unfortunately, a whopping 65% of those responding to the survey said that their mental health has suffered because of their job and the long hours – and that's for those who are still employed. A full third of respondents have been laid off in the last two years, with two-thirds of that group saying they were laid off in the past year. And sadly, more than half (54%) of those who've been laid off have yet to find another job, though not for a lack of trying: 62% say they've applied for 20 or more jobs, with over a quarter (27%) saying they've applied for over a hundred. Overall, one-fifth of survey respondents (21%) are unemployed, up from 13% in the last report.

The next Game Developers Conference: Festival of Gaming will take place in San Francisco on March 1–4, 2027.

articles.title: Distributed Ray Tracer
articles.content:
Hey HN, I'm Julius, I'm a backend engineer at Hatchet and created this demo to show off some of Hatchet's new features, primarily durable streams and serverless endpoints. Those, however, are just background details that made this significantly easier to scale. By distributing the rendering across many different nodes, orchestrated using Hatchet, it makes it possible to render quite high fidelity scenes fairly quickly. All of this would be possible on a single machine, but would be much slower without dedicated hardware (RT cores, etc). The renderer itself is using well-known ray tracing techniques, with no special considerations there. The renderer is a slightly modified version of https://github.com/ekzhang/rpt, with additional support for SDF scripting using https://docs.rs/fidget/latest/fidget/. SDFs have been popular in the demoscene community, though perhaps not super well known outside of that, and are capable of creating some fantastic looking scenes: https://www.shadertoy.com/view/ld3Gz2. The coolest part here is using a DSL to represent the SDFs in a rendering pipeline, and using LLMs with a chat interface to create them. The source is available here: https://github.com/hatchet-dev/distributed-ray-tracer

articles.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
articles.description: Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics. Shame about the privately bit
articles.content:
With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms.

In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc.

But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products.

The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028.

"I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said.

Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance.

"My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot."

All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio.

Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you."

They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir, while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants.

Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power, and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority."

At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter.

It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process.

Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company.

He told CNBC: " If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir. Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection."

In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough.

"And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet.

Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight.

Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®

articles.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
articles.description: A little tinkering can black hole obnoxious Samsung TV ads and some tracking, until a firmware fix ruins the fun
articles.content:
eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined.

Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television.

Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back.

First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month, eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort.

eMudhra has since left the CA racket, saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue.

What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of.

eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing.

By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task.

“Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.”

The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers.

As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work.

“It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo.

It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads.

“The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.”

As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself.

“I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained.

We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

articles.title: Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data
articles.content:
Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo ( https://leeroo.com/ ). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso ( https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso ), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run. The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation. For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions. The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox. We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack. You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs Here’s how it works… Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it. For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject. After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic. kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new ), and compound over that by running experimentations. We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results… - Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model ( https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/ ). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model. - ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems ( https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107 ). - AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems ( https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re... ). We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia ( https://leeroopedia.com/ ): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents. If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help! https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso

articles.title: Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.”
articles.description: At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to The post Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.” appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to release patched PHP images before an agreed-upon embargo with other partners had lifted.

When Chainguard shipped patched PHP container images more than six hours ahead of an October 21 coordinated security release, PHP’s maintainers accused the company of giving attackers a head start. Chainguard argues attackers already had one.

Chainguard founder and CTO Matt Moore

In an interview with The New Stack, Moore said, “We own the decision that we chose to do it. Nobody could force us to do it — but we did not do it in a vacuum.” He also described, in discussions with TNS, other participants in the embargo and security vendors’ reports of activity targeting the vulnerabilities before Chainguard released its images.

Chainguard was not saying that they patched it faster so they shipped it first. According to Moore, Chainguard believed attackers could already exploit the bugs, or were at least close to figuring out how — or were trying to figure it out.

The two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), collectively known as PHP2Shell, were serious memory-management and error-handling flaws. Under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker could execute code on a PHP server.

The two bugs involved PHP’s handling of memory exhaustion and its failure to clear references to freed memory between requests. In the first, reaching a memory limit at the wrong moment could interrupt PHP before it finished setting up internal data. Later processing could mistake that unfinished data for valid information. In the second vulnerability, an error could leave PHP holding a reference to memory from an earlier request that had already been freed. A subsequent request could then access that invalid memory. Under exploitable conditions, these failures could let an attacker run code inside the server’s PHP process.

Researchers demonstrated remote code execution through both Apache/mod_php and application-level PHP-FPM paths for the first vulnerability, and against a real-world Apache/mod_php application for the second.

These were problems in PHP itself, not something an administrator could fix by simply updating a WordPress plugin. It was a fundamental and nasty security hole.

How bad were the flaws?

PHP’s advisories rate both vulnerabilities 9.2, or critical, under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0. Exploitability depends on the PHP build, server configuration, extensions, and application behavior. The advisories do not establish that every PHP installation can be compromised. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. The potential exposure is substantial: As of November 11, W3Techs reported that PHP powered 68.8% of websites whose server-side programming language it could identify.

According to the PHP Foundation’s account, a developer investigating issues from a 2024 security audit spotted the out-of-memory problem, but no concrete attack path was established then. Proposed fixes risked compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service problems, or changes across PHP extensions.

On August 11, Calif researcher Ryan A. reported remote code execution from the same underlying problem. From that date, fixing it became the PHP Foundation security team’s top priority. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying flaw. Wiz supplied additional attack vectors on August 24, and OpenAI reported more on September 18.

How the PHP security patch came apart

In response, PHP’s maintainers coordinated fixes with researchers and distributors. Then details about the release process began leaking.

On October 20, the CVE identifiers circulated publicly, accompanied by an incorrect release time and severity score. PHP responded by issuing a warning and moving the release forward a day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Calif, one of the reporting security companies, then mistakenly published a video demonstrating its proof of concept. Although the video was deleted, copies circulated. PHP also acknowledged that mitigation advice given to critical infrastructure providers might have leaked.

In short, the information environment was already a mess before Chainguard published anything.

But the PHP Foundation maintained that its remaining coordination window still served a purpose: specifically that distributors were packaging the fixes, and releasing immediately would leave many users without a straightforward update path. At 07:41 UTC on October 21, Chainguard published its patched images anyway — six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed-upon time.

The PHP Foundation criticized this move: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” That meant, it argued, that “any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release.”

A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

That was the PHP Foundation’s central objection. A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

Moore’s defense: The advantage had already shifted to the attackers

Moore doesn’t dispute that releasing patched binaries can help attackers. He argues that, by then, the advantage an embargo was supposed to preserve had already eroded.

While defenders alone know about a vulnerability, he told The New Stack, confidentiality gives them time to prepare. Once attackers have enough information to exploit it, withholding available fixes can reverse that advantage: attackers can act, while users outside the embargo cannot protect themselves.

“If we see exploitation in the wild, it’s incumbent upon us to release it,” Moore said. In his account, reports from other security vendors were what pushed Chainguard toward that conclusion.

Moore said Chainguard learned on the Friday before the release that PHP had a vulnerability, pointed its vulnerability-hunting harness at the software, and found the vulnerability or produced a proof of concept within hours. That is Chainguard’s account of its own research. But it helps explain the company’s thinking in breaking the embargo: If your tools can find the bug quickly, you have to consider whether attackers’ tools can too.

He also disputed the implication that Chainguard simply went off on its own. According to Moore, other embargo participants woke Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc to discuss the situation while PHP maintainers in Europe were asleep. Moore declined to identify those participants.

Moore accepted that Chainguard made the final decision. It does, however, distinguish the company’s account of a disputed emergency decision from an account in which it ignored everyone else without discussion.

The evidence supports concern, not certainty

Public evidence supports Chainguard’s concern that attackers were already targeting the flaws. For example, Amazon Threat Intelligence reported a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It also reported proof-of-concept exploits beginning around 02:00 UTC on October 21, followed by additional attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. Some of that activity clearly preceded Chainguard’s 07:41 release.

Cloudflare likewise reported observing attack traffic targeting its customers before the official release. It said its free and paid web application firewall protections were enabled by default starting at 03:02 UTC on October 21.

So, no, Chainguard was not imagining hostile interest in these bugs.

But Amazon included an important qualification: “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.” The PHP security team, meanwhile, said it examined the circulating proofs of concept and “did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.”

Those statements are not necessarily contradictory. A honeypot can record a request intended to exploit a vulnerability without establishing that it can achieve remote code execution against a real application. Likewise, PHP’s failure to find a functional public exploit does not prove that no attacker privately possessed one.

Subsequent evidence should not be confused with what was known that morning. On October 26, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That confirms exploitation was known by then; it does not establish when the first successful compromise occurred or whether Chainguard’s early release enabled it.

Welcome to security incident response. The evidence rarely arrives neatly labeled.

Did the binaries give attackers something they lacked?

Moore’s second argument is narrower. Attackers were already probing the relevant code, so publishing patched binaries might not have helped much.

“I don’t see any evidence that what we did helped the attackers in ways that they didn’t already have,” he told TNS. He acknowledged that comparing patched and unpatched binaries can identify vulnerable code, including with AI-assisted disassembly. But identifying the code, he argued, isn’t necessarily the same as building a working exploit.

Fair enough. Locating a memory-corruption bug and reliably turning it into remote code execution are different engineering problems.

Still, this defense has limits. Evidence that some attackers knew where to look does not establish that every prospective attacker did. Nor does it establish that the patch contained no useful clues beyond the vulnerability’s location. Chainguard’s argument depends on how much actionable information was already available and how reliable it was.

The same restraint applies to the accusation against Chainguard. Publishing the binaries created an opportunity to study the changes. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that a particular compromise happened because Chainguard released early.

The two sides were assessing different risks. Chainguard emphasized the danger of withholding a ready patch from users while hostile activity was visible. PHP emphasized the danger of distributing new information before the wider ecosystem could update. Both risks were real.

AI makes the timing problem worse

The broader concern is that AI-assisted vulnerability research could shorten the time defenders have to respond. The public reports cited here do not establish whether the pre-release PHP2Shell attempts used AI, or that this was the first incident of its kind.

For Moore, the PHP dispute fits a larger problem: attackers’ ability to turn vulnerability information into an exploit may outrun defenders’ ability to build and distribute a fix.

He described a scenario in which a Chromium patch becomes public, and an attacker develops an exploit faster than it takes to compile the browser. That was a warning about where the industry is heading, not a claim that this exact scenario had occurred.

“You literally cannot produce builds fast enough,” he said. And the build is only the beginning. Even if Chainguard produces an updated image quickly, customers still have to incorporate it, rebuild their applications, test them, and deploy.

Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

That is the uncomfortable part of the “patch faster” answer. Faster is useful. Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

Moore’s proposed longer-term response is to reduce the number of vulnerabilities that require this race in the first place. articles.title: Google built an AI model that can’t write a sentence — and that’s the point
articles.description: Google’s new Gemini Decisions API, introduced Wednesday, is designed to handle the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of The post Google built an AI model that can’t write a sentence — and that’s the point appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Google’s new Gemini Decisions API, introduced Wednesday, is designed to handle the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs, and faster response times than traditional generative models.

…the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs and faster response times than traditional generative models.

Instead of using a generative model to work through each decision and produce a text response, the API uses a new model, Gemini Decision 1, to evaluate predefined options in a single pass.

According to Google, response times range from 150 to 250 milliseconds for tested workloads, while pricing starts at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output-token charges.

The release comes just weeks after OpenAI launched its own Decisions API, joining TypeSafe AI and Microsoft in a growing market for models built to make specific decisions without generating text.

One pass, no generated text

The API supports a 256,000-token context window and can evaluate up to 1,000 independent questions against a single input, including multimodal content. Its responses include probabilities and confidence scores that developers can use to select between predefined options, evaluate information against specific criteria and decide how an application should proceed.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai described the model in a post on X as “built for closed-set choices,” while Google DeepMind product manager Min Choi and principal scientist Felix Yu characterized the API as providing “purpose-built primitives for bounded choices” in the launch announcement.

Where Google already uses it

Google is already using the model internally, including in Gemini Notebook, where real-time model and reasoning-level routing has reportedly reduced latency by up to 40%. Google Search also uses it to detect potentially adversarial behavior involving MCP tools.

Benchmarks come from Google

Google’s benchmark results show Gemini Decision 1 outperforming OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, although the competition with TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 is closer.

Logan Kilpatrick, who leads product for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, described it on X as “our new frontier decision model in the Gemini API.” On JevBench, Google’s model scored 92.2%, compared with 90.9% for Luna and 90% for Jev.

But Jev came out ahead on two of the seven shared tests and was cheaper to run, costing $0.68 for the full benchmark suite compared with $0.88 for Gemini Decision 1. Google’s model also recorded the lowest calibration error among those tested.

All of the benchmark figures come from Google’s own testing, and independent evaluations have yet to establish how the models compare in production. SiliconANGLE also noted that Jev is cheaper than Google’s model on a per-token basis.

All of the benchmark figures come from Google’s own testing, and independent evaluations have yet to establish how the models compare in production.

What developers actually pay

Developers only pay to send the shared context once, even when they’re asking multiple questions about it, although the questions themselves still count toward token usage. The API evaluates each question separately, so a workflow that needs to use one answer to decide what to ask next requires another call.

Gemini Decision 1 is available through Google AI Studio, with a free prototyping tier and integrations through OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, and LiteLLM. Support for Gemini on Google Cloud is also planned, although Google has not announced a release date.

articles.title: Microsoft has an image problem with November's Windows security update
articles.description: Zero-size graphics can derail printing, while some admins also face activation failures
articles.content:
Printing with Windows has always been something of a choose-your-own-adventure, and November's security update has added another unwelcome plot twist: documents containing certain images might not print.

The issue affects images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution. These might not be visible to users, but can form part of a document's watermarking or layout.

After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected."

According to the notification (WI1549472), most versions of Windows are affected, from the latest Windows 11 26H2 through Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016. Windows Server from 2025 to 2016 is also affected.

Users need not have added these objects themselves. Microsoft says document-generation tools can insert them even when no graphic is visible.

Printer problems aren't the only issue requiring attention. After installation of the November 2026 security update, Microsoft warned that "certain Windows activation and licensing operations performed using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail."

This one is a little more niche, but it could be a headache for affected administrators. It primarily affects organizations that use command-line tools or automated processes to manage Windows activation and licensing.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter ( SWbemObjectEx ), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said. "The failure has been observed while executing the command ' slmgr.vbs /skms-domain ' and ' slmgr.vbs /ipk '."

The notice (WI1549486) currently lists Windows 11 23H2, Windows 10 22H2 and 21H2, and Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019 as affected.

The printing problem remains under investigation, but Microsoft says a fix for the activation issue is due in the coming days. Administrators needing an interim workaround must contact Microsoft Support for Business. ®

articles.title: President Trump says Apple’s Tim Cook is the only man to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
articles.description: President Trump says Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump has said that retired Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, just hours after it was announced that the latter had resigned in the wake of a series of scandals. Taking to his Truth Social platform, the President said, "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! President DONALD J. TRUMP."

Nvidia's board of directors announced on Wednesday that Huang had resigned following the revelation that he conducted an extramarital affair with a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and a further affair with Nvidia Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell.

Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, will serve as Interim CEO while the company looks for a replacement. Naturally, names have been floated as potential successor candidates, including Apple's Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji.

With Nvidia at the center of the global explosion in AI, Huang and Trump have enjoyed a close relationship that routinely makes news headlines. Trump previously described Huang as 'utterly visionary' in regard to his views on tariffs and rescinding President Biden's AI Diffusion Rule.

President Trump's name has been mentioned in the ongoing Huang affair scandal. Notably, it is alleged that while U.S. intelligence believed that Huang had been the target of a Chinese honeypot operation, reports claim that President Trump was briefed on the matter but chose not to do anything with the information, so as not to affect Nvidia's sales or antagonize China.

Congress has summoned Jensen Huang to appear before the Select Committee on the CCP, with lawmakers threatening to issue Huang with a subpoena if he doesn't agree to attend a closed-door meeting voluntarily.

Tim Cook is currently the Executive Chair of Apple's board, having served as the company's CEO from 2011 to 2026. During his tenure, he oversaw the launch of a plethora of Apple services, including Apple Music and Apple TV, while expanding into new product categories such as Apple Watch and AirPods.

Nvidia's share price plunged more than 10 percentage points at the open on Wednesday, but recovered much of that ground as traders looked to take advantage of the dip in Nvidia's share price. The company will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results next week, on Tuesday, November 17.

articles.title: Elon Musk says it ‘would be an honor’ to hire ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.description: A random X poster urged Elon Musk to hire Jensen Huang just hours before the former Nvidia chief resigned from his position.
articles.content:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO two weeks after his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was revealed by intelligence sources and a day after his affair with an Nvidia vice president became publicly known. But hours before this move, when it was just rumored that the Nvidia board was planning to oust him, Elon Musk had already stated his willingness to hire the former Nvidia chief on X. A random X user posted, “Elon please hire Jensen,” to which the billionaire replied, “That would be an honor.”

@zerohedge That would be an honor November 12, 2026

Despite the scandals that Jensen is currently facing, he still has the engineering know-how, deep knowledge of the industry and its inner workings, plus multiple connections across the world, which would be extremely valuable for any company looking to break into the semiconductor industry.

This is exactly what Elon Musk is doing with his Terafab project, which he first mentioned in November 2025. Jensen Huang even warned that this was going to be a challenge, pointing out that “the engineering, the science, and the artistry of doing what TSMC does for a living is extremely hard.” Nevertheless, Musk poured his resources into the project, with construction on the Terafab facility in full swing and with plans to hit volume chip production by the second half of 2028. Musk himself said that the site targets a production capacity of a million wafers a month by 2032. Tesla has an ambitious AI accelerator roadmap, and SpaceX has even touted making its own GPUs in the future.

We still don’t know what Jensen Huang’s plans are, but even though he’s no longer a part of the Nvidia board and its leadership, Jensen and his wife, Lori, still jointly own approximately 800 million Nvidia shares through various trusts and LLCs, while Huang himself personally owns around 70 million Nvidia shares.

Aside from that, he still has an outstanding invitation from Congress to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols, which could turn into a subpoena if he snubs them, although we don’t know how his resignation would affect the closed-door meeting. There’s also a reported FBI investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive who was allegedly instrumental in the import of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China and is suspected of working with China’s Ministry of State Security.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in the long list of executives who resigned or were ousted from their leadership position because of a relationship or an affair with a subordinate. This includes former Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher in 2005, HP CEO Mark Hurd in 2010, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in 2018, and former McDonald’s CEO Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Musk himself is known to have had relationships with subordinates from his various companies, and that he has even fathered four children with Shivon Zilis, a top executive at Neuralink who started working at Tesla in 2017, through IVF.

It’s still not confirmed if Musk’s reply is a serious offer for Jensen Huang. But if the former Nvidia chief ever decides to work for Musk on his Terafab project, then Jensen could put his effort and expertise into turning it into a formidable competitor to Nvidia.

articles.title: United Airlines wants you to check in, not your chatbot
articles.description: AI agents face restrictions over safety checks that require a human touch
articles.content:
United Airlines has become the latest company to slap restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, warning that the bots could make unintended purchases, expose customer data, or bypass checks requiring human acknowledgment.

The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.

United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind.

And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems.

AI agents are pitched as a way to outsource life's minutiae, and it's difficult to navigate the web without tripping over a breathless influencer explaining why you need one, or dozens, or hundreds of virtual personal assistants.

The thing is that operating these assistants requires care and thought. Earlier this year, British mathematician Professor Hannah Fry conducted a cautionary experiment in which she gave an AI agent a bank card, and a bit too much agency, to see what it would do. Passwords were coughed up, and some ill-considered purchases were made. Still, as Fry said of the agent, dubbed Cassandra, "don't let her incompetence fool you, because these things are getting better fast."

Last month, reports emerged of major US banks blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside accounts and taking actions on behalf of the customer. This month, several UK banks were reported to have followed suit.

United stated: "Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety."

The Register asked United Airlines how it planned to implement the blocking. There are a few options, including physical biometric confirmation for actions or checking for signs of automated browser driving. Amazon has also moved against unauthorized AI agents, blocking Meta's Muse (the "AI that gets it done," according to Meta's marketing) in September.

The airline has yet to respond. ®

articles.title: The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery
articles.description: For decades, enterprise vulnerability management ran on human time: A security researcher manually dissected a binary, traced execution paths, built The post The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
For decades, enterprise vulnerability management ran on human time: A security researcher manually dissected a binary, traced execution paths, built a proof of concept, and filed a coordinated disclosure. Engineering leads evaluated the CVSS score and prioritized the fi before working it into an upcoming sprint schedule. Then, finally, they shipped the update.

That deliberate cadence is a thing of the past.

In the first nine months of 2026, publishers recorded 75,242 CVEs, representing roughly 20% of all vulnerabilities published since the CVE program was established in 1999.

The acceleration is steepening: according to the Cyber Strategy Institute, nearly 38,000 of those flaws surfaced in Q3 alone.

“The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.”

The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.

Why vulnerabilities exploded in 2026

This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.

Autonomous codebase traversal: Legacy SAST tools flooded dashboards with noisy pattern matches. Modern agentic security systems run full-context semantic analysis: cloning repositories, tracing asynchronous data flows across microservices, constructing dynamic exploit payloads in sandboxes, and confirming exploitability before ever raising an alert.

Exhaustive compute at scale: Compute does not tire. Swarms of automated agents continuously traverse open-source package registries and public repositories, decompiling transitive dependencies, auditing legacy C/C++ utilities, and testing modern Go, Rust, and Node.js runtimes for concurrency bugs, deserialization flaws, and memory leaks.

Focus on foundational infrastructure: Autonomous discovery focuses heavily on high-leverage software targets, identity layers, reverse proxies, parsers, and container runtimes.

“This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.”

When machines search exhaustively across the entire public software graph, they will discover every reachable flaw.

The operational cascade

The deluge of machine-discovered CVEs creates severe structural friction across risk management, engineering velocity, and compliance:

The exposure gap becomes unmanageable: As detailed in analysis on the expanding CVE exposure gap, the critical hazard is the elapsed time between public exploit discovery and downstream production deployment. When agentic frameworks generate working zero-day or N-day exploits within hours of a code push, a multi-day patching window is an open door.

Alert paralysis and triage debt: Engineering teams are trapped between CVSS scores (which measure theoretical severity) and EPSS metrics (which predict real-world exploitation likelihood). Discerning whether an alert represents an unreachable helper function or an active, weaponizable zero-click flaw has turned routine triage into continuous crisis management.

Compliance and audit deadlock: Frameworks like NIST SP 800-53 (Control SI-2), PCI-DSS 4.0, and DORA enforce strict timelines for critical and high-severity issues. When 9.0+ CVSS scores arrive in weekly batches, security and platform leads spend more time writing risk-acceptance waivers than hardening production architecture.

Can internal IT teams keep up with patching and push innovation?

The short answer is no.

Enterprise development exists to deliver business value: ship differentiated features, enhance platform reliability, and expand market share.

Yet today’s software supply chains rely on thousands of dependencies. When a critical flaw lands in foundational infrastructure, such as an authentication engine, an API gateway, or a database driver, feature roadmaps freeze. Development teams are forced into fire drills:

Halt active sprint work.

Trace internal dependencies to determine real exploitability.

Reconcile dependency breaks, merge conflicts, and integration regressions.

Execute emergency deployments across multi-region production clusters.

Defending against automated, machine-speed discovery using manual human labor is an economic dead end.

The architectural shift: Decoupling architecture from maintenance

Open-source software (OSS) remains a foundation of enterprise computing, but self-hosting foundational components introduces an unsustainable operational tax: you become the de facto maintainer of every layer you host.

To withstand the automated vulnerability era, forward-looking engineering teams are changing their operating model: preserve open standards and architectures, but outsource the patching burden.

1. Managed platform tiers for critical edge and identity

Foundational edge components, such as identity and authorization planes (e.g., Ory Kratos/Hydra) or ingress proxies (e.g., Envoy), form an organization’s perimeter. When implementation flaws or protocol vulnerabilities hit these layers, maintaining self-hosted community forks requires constant emergency rebuilds. Shifting these layers to managed vendor clouds offloads zero-day mitigation, regression testing, and upstream backporting to teams dedicated entirely to that software layer.

2. Commercial subscriptions with contractual backporting SLAs

For organizations restricted by strict data sovereignty, air-gapped data centers, or zero-trust VPC policies, public SaaS is not always an option. However, relying purely on raw community repositories leaves internal teams subject to unpredictable release cycles and breaking updates.

A viable hybrid approach is adopting commercial open-source enterprise subscriptions backed by formal CVE remediation SLAs (such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux, enterprise distributions of Kubernetes, or commercial licenses like the Ory Enterprise License ). Organizations retain full control over their data plane while outsourcing patch engineering:

Predictable remediation SLAs: Contractual response windows for High and Critical vulnerabilities replace upstream community best-effort timelines.

Non-breaking LTS backports: Vendors backport security fixes directly to long-term support branches, eliminating the breaking schema changes and API refactors that accompany major upstream updates.

Verified distribution streams: Access to signed SBOMs and hardened enterprise container images reduces internal triage friction in CI/CD pipelines.

3. Continuous delivery automation and runtime shielding

For internally maintained services, teams must automate the path from patch to production. This requires pairing automated GitOps workflows (e.g., ArgoCD, Renovate) with progressive deployment controllers (like Flagger or Argo Rollouts) and eBPF-based runtime shielding (such as Cilium Tetragon). Automated canary verification and kernel-level network enforcement isolate vulnerabilities in flight, buying engineers time to test and deploy updates without emergency rollouts.

Fighting automation with automation

The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. As autonomous models and agentic fuzzing advance, exploit discovery and weaponization will move faster still.

“The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden.”

Attempting to absorb this flood with manual Jira tickets and emergency weekend deployments guarantees developer burnout and security breaches. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden, allowing internal engineering teams to focus on what matters… shipping product.
